33 A metal wire has a length of 2.50 m and a cross-sectional area of 4.50  10–6
m2. The resistivity of
the metal is 3.50  10–7
 m.
The wire is stretched so that its length increases to 2.65 m. The wire remains cylindrical and the
volume of the wire remains constant.
What is the change in the resistance of the wire?
A
0.012 
B
0.024 
C
0.19 
D
0.22 

hints: Notice the volume $V = AL$ stays constant while length grows from $2.50 \text{ m}$ to $2.65 \text{ m}$, so the new area $A_2$ must be smaller than $4.50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$.
Recall $R = \rho L / A$ and $V = A_1 L_1 = A_2 L_2$, so resistance can be written as $R = \rho L^2 / V$ and increases faster than length alone.
Calculate $R_1$ first, then find $A_2 = A_1 L_1 / L_2$ and $R_2$, and finally subtract to get the increase in resistance.
walkthrough: Find the original resistance using $R = \rho L / A$. $R_1 = (3.50 \times 10^{-7} \times 2.50) / (4.50 \times 10^{-6}) \approx 0.194 \text{ } \Omega$.
Use constant volume to find the new area. $V = A_1 L_1 = 4.50 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.50 = 1.125 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^3$.
Calculate $A_2 = V / L_2 = (1.125 \times 10^{-5}) / 2.65 \approx 4.25 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$, showing the wire gets thinner.
Find the change $\Delta R = R_2 - R_1 \approx 0.218 - 0.194 \approx 0.024 \text{ } \Omega$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This is $\rho \Delta L / A$ with $A$ kept constant, so it ignores that stretching with constant volume must reduce the cross-sectional area.

B.explanation: This is $R_2 - R_1$ when $R = \rho L/A$ is used with $A_2 = V/L_2$ from constant volume, giving about $0.024 \text{ } \Omega$.

C.explanation: This is approximately the original resistance $R_1 = \rho \times 2.50 / (4.50 \times 10^{-6})$, not the change $R_2 - R_1$.

D.explanation: This is approximately the new resistance $R_2$ after stretching, not the change $R_2 - R_1$.
